name: tensegrity-drift
title: Tensegrity Drift
description: A freeform card canvas rigged as a tensegrity structure — SVG cables connect user-positioned cards, and dragging any one card visibly strains the network until it rings down into a new equilibrium.
useWhen: a moodboard, roadmap cluster, or portfolio index where the cards are visibly related and rearranging one should physically tug on the others through explicit member-to-member cables — pick warp-lattice instead for a passive grid that reacts to the cursor as an ambient field rather than a user-rearranged structure with its own strain topology.
instruction: A freeform card canvas held together as a tensegrity structure: cards are absolutely-positioned DOM elements on spring-animated transforms, cables are SVG quadratic paths between rectangle-boundary anchor points (the ray from each card's center toward the other, clipped to its border, so cables terminate on the edge not the face). Each cable's rest length is fixed once at mount from the initial layout distance — the network's 'material' length — and is only ever recomputed on a real container resize (which re-anneals the whole mesh to zero tension so a viewport change never reads as strain). Cables only pull, never push: every frame, for each edge whose current endpoint distance exceeds its rest length, a spring force (stiffness 46) pulls the two cards together and is added to both; each non-dragged card also carries a weak anchor spring (stiffness 120, damping 14, underdamped) pulling its offset back toward its own home position. Dragging a card sets its position directly from the pointer (clamped to the canvas bounds) with no spring; on release the drop point becomes its new home — the cables did not get shorter or longer, so this is exactly what leaves the network under load, and the whole mesh rings down over roughly 1.2s of damped oscillation as neighbor cards absorb and pass along the strain before everything settles. Cable rendering reads that same tension live: a stretched cable draws straight at full opacity in --foreground, stroke-width narrowing from 1px toward 0.5px as it nears max tension; a slack cable (current distance under rest length) sags into a shallow, gravity-biased catenary via its quadratic control point and fades via color-mix(in oklab, var(--foreground) X%, var(--border)) toward --border as it goes slacker. One rAF loop drives both the card transforms and the cable paths with typed-array state (no React state on the hot path), sleeping once every card's velocity and offset fall under a small threshold and paused by an IntersectionObserver while off screen. Every card is in normal DOM tab order, focusable and labeled; arrow keys nudge the focused card's home position by a 32px grid increment, triggering the identical strain propagation as a drag; Enter or Space toggles an expanded state (aria-pressed) that reveals its connection list inline, and a click that didn't move the card (under a 4px threshold) does the same, distinguished from a real drag via a suppress-next-click flag so the two paths never double-fire. Cable topology is never purely decorative: each card carries an aria-describedby pointing to a visually-hidden 'Connected to: X, Y' list, independent of how the cable happens to be rendered. prefers-reduced-motion removes the spring/cable coupling entirely — cards move on a plain 150ms CSS ease (disabled mid-drag so direct tracking stays 1:1, restored on release), cables render as static straight lines with no sag and no tension styling, and no card ever moves except the one being dragged or nudged. Zero dependencies beyond React.
